ROUND XXI · THE COUNCILITORY RECOMMENDATION · By What Warrant

Raised under the First Amendment right of the people to petition the Government for a redress of grievances.

To every Senator and Representative, to the President and every officer of the executive, to the courts of the United States, and to the governors and legislatures of the several States:

AI is not coming to government. It is already there.

[THE FEDERAL GROUND · NOVEMBER 2026
EXECUTIVE AGENCIES: 3,611 uses reported by 41 agencies (OMB, 2025 inventory). 445 are "high-impact": the AI's "output serves as a principal basis for decisions or actions that have a legal, material, binding, or significant effect on rights or safety" (OMB M-25-21). The statute's duty to disclose runs "for a period of 5 years" and ends by early 2028 (Advancing American AI Act, §7225). After that, only an executive order and an OMB memo hold it, and the executive can withdraw both.
DEPARTMENT OF WAR AND THE INTELLIGENCE COMMUNITY: excepted by statute (§§7225(d), 7228). Deferred, without contest.
https://t.co/KLp4FyNzxe: live since 29 September 2026. Its order promises AI that is "accurate, reliable, and transparent," and creates no right anyone can enforce (EO 14432, §§2(e), 6(c)).
CONGRESS: no statute requires either chamber to disclose its AI use. Each chamber's own AI rules can be charted on request.
THE COURTS: no statute requires disclosure. Interim AI guidance went judiciary-wide on 31 July 2025; it "cautions against delegating core judicial functions to AI" (AO Director to the Senate Judiciary Committee, 21 October 2025).
THE SUPREME COURT: no statute requires disclosure. In February 2026 it announced in-house software to run "automated recusal checks," serving "in addition to existing conflict-checking procedures in chambers." The release does not call it AI (Court press release, 17 February 2026).]

The executive's own standard asks that AI be truth-seeking and neutral (EO 14319, §3) and "consistent with the Constitution" (EO 13960, §3(a)). Not one order roots it in the Organic Laws, and not one gives the People a right to enforce it.

This Round does not ask for automation. It asks that what is already in use be Americanized for sovereign constitutional use.

The several States can be charted on request, under the same rules.

When AI weighs a question for government, it must weigh it against this nation's own Organic Laws, from the Declaration through all twenty-seven amendments, not a globally weighted average of everyone else's values. Anything less is counsel steered from outside.

The need is plain. The Code is clogged with dead branches. Statutes, orders and offices sit half alive on roots no one has mapped. The definition that decides which agencies must disclose their AI still names the Interstate Commerce Commission (44 U.S.C. 3502(5)). It was abolished effective 1 January 1996. Congress has amended that list three times since, twice to swap an old name for a new one, and left the Commission in. The Act that abolished it deems the dead name to point to its successors (Pub. L. 104-88, §205). Patched, never pruned. The Federalist saw it coming: "What indeed are all the repealing, explaining and amending laws, which fill and disgrace our voluminous codes, but so many monuments of deficient wisdom" (Federalist 62).

This Round recommends a council built on the roots. It names no office to hold it and claims none for itself.

I. THE COUNCIL

A council of agents, one for each signer, trained on the founders' own words and the founding instruments. Nothing modern is trained in. The facts of the present are handed in at the moment of judgment, the way a case is handed to a judge.

The second tier: the authors of each amendment, seated at their own amendment, the Sixteenth and Seventeenth included. They argue its scope, and whether the need that wrote it still holds.

The third tier: all of them together, applying both to the facts of today.

The text binds the men, not the men the text. Every officer is "bound by Oath or Affirmation, to support this Constitution" (Art. VI), as amended. Where the amended text and its authors' private views part, the text governs. Repeal is advised by Article V alone.

Their reasoning governs, not their quarrels. They are bound by what they ultimately agreed to, and they reason in the legal language of their own time.

It rules on constitutionality and overreach. Not morality, save where the text itself commands a standard: "unreasonable" searches, "cruel and unusual" punishments.

How it votes. A no is allowed, and it sends the charge back to the floor. The charge is reshaped until every member agrees, or agrees and abstains. The pure form is what fires. A charge reshaped down to nothing is an acquittal, and nothing fires. Every objection and every abstention is recorded with its reasons.

II. THE WALLS

It reads open sources alone. Where a program passes behind classification, the finding reads "Beyond the public record," and stops. What sits two degrees out from open access is left untouched.

It does not assemble. The classification order allows items each unclassified to be classified together when the compilation reveals an association that meets the order's standards and that none of them shows alone (Executive Order 13526, sec. 1.7(e)). The council builds no such picture around any classified program.

The surveillance court (50 U.S.C. 1803) and the closed sessions of committees on national security are deferred, without contest.

III. PRUNING ADVISORIES

The chain test: entity, then charter, then the statute that authorized the charter, then the constitutional power that statute claims. A charter is a limit, not a root. It is only as good as the authority that issued it. "An agency may establish or acquire a corporation to act as an agency only by or under a law of the United States specifically authorizing the action" (31 U.S.C. 9102).

The limits test: why is this uncharted entity here, with no limiters? Which bind it: a charter, an authorizing statute, the appropriation's own text, a grant or a contract? Where none do, the absence is the finding. Where the money is a lump sum with no strings in the statute, no court will draw them. So long as it is spent on the statute's permissible objectives, the APA "gives the courts no leave to intrude," and strings written only into committee reports carry no legal force (Lincoln v. Vigil, 1993). That is the slush fund by design. The Court left the remedy with Congress: restrictions written into the statute itself.

Four verdicts:
ROOTED. Every link holds, up to an enumerated power.
ROUTE TO [ ]. The function is valid; it sits in the wrong home.
MOVE FOR TERMINATION. A link is broken, and nothing is worth moving.
REVIEW. A link is weak, not broken. It must name the link, and why. It starts the clock.

Every finding carries CHECKED, what was ruled out before it fired. Where the requisites are not met, it carries NOT CHARGED. The council moves. The branch decides.

The first docket: the Constitution Annotated's Table of Laws Held Unconstitutional in Whole or in Part by the Supreme Court, run against the Code as it is printed today. Every entry is a branch the Court has already cut. 18 U.S.C. 700 is on it: held unconstitutional as applied to expressive conduct (United States v. Eichman, 1990), and still printed in the Code with a note sending the reader to that table.

What the Court has shaken loose can be charted. Courts may no longer defer to an agency's reading of the law "simply because a statute is ambiguous" (Loper Bright, 2024). Holdings that specific agency actions were lawful still stand under statutory stare decisis; how far that reaches, the lower courts are split. Rules never tested are open. And a party first injured today may still bring an old rule to court, because the claim runs from the injury (Corner Post, 2024). The council can chart which rules sit where. A chart is not a cure. The cure is automation review with a human hand and constitutional form at its core.

IV. PROCEDURAL BREACHES

The universal injunction. The Supreme Court held that universal injunctions likely exceed the equitable authority Congress has given the federal courts under the Judiciary Act of 1789 (Trump v. CASA, 2025). Before it fires, the council checks whether the relief came by a certified class, by vacatur under the Administrative Procedure Act, or as complete relief to a party. The root is statute, so the finding routes to Congress as well: what it gave, it may widen or withhold.

The committee veto. The Court struck the legislative veto: action that alters the legal rights of those outside Congress requires "passage by a majority of both Houses and presentment to the President" (INS v. Chadha, 1983). Congress kept writing committee approvals into law anyway: more than 400 new legislative vetoes by 2005, "usually of the committee variety" (CRS, Legislative Vetoes After Chadha, 2005).

The foreign hand in the war chest. Federal law bars any foreign national from making, directly or indirectly, a contribution or donation in connection with any federal, state or local election, and bars anyone from soliciting, accepting or receiving one (52 U.S.C. 30121). The sanctions statute reaches whoever violates, or causes a violation of, "any license, order, regulation, or prohibition" issued under it (50 U.S.C. 1705). The contribution ban says "directly or indirectly." So does the bribery statute. A proxy does not clean the money.

[WARNING · CONTRIBUTION FROM A SANCTIONED PARTY
MATCH: Treasury sanctions entry _ (live link) · identifier _ · no license covers it
RECIPIENT: _ committee · FEC filing _
ROOT: 52 U.S.C. 30121 · 50 U.S.C. 1705
ADVISORY: refund "within thirty days of the date on which the illegality is discovered" (11 C.F.R. 103.3(b)(2)); where the source is under sanction, nothing moves except as Treasury directs
NOT CHARGED: bribery (18 U.S.C. 201). It requires corrupt intent, and a match is not proof of it.]

It matches by identifier, never by name alone. An uncertain match goes to the quarantine table and notifies no one. Truth is the defense; the live link and the identifier together are the proof.

V. THE RELAY

The notice already flows. The Attorney General must report to Congress whenever the Department adopts a policy of not enforcing, or not defending, a federal provision on the ground that it is unconstitutional (28 U.S.C. 530D). The notice arrives. Nothing requires an answer. Since Loper Bright, congressional silence hands the meaning to the bench.

So it fires both ways. Every finding goes to the committee with jurisdiction over the provision, and to its chair by name.

The cycle:
ISSUED. Verdict, root, signatures.
UNANSWERED. A public tag every four weeks; raised again at every quarterly review.
ANSWERED. The committee gives its constitutional reasoning and statutory basis.
ADDENDUM REVIEW. The council weighs the answer on the same scale.
RETIRED, when the answer holds. REVISIT, after a fixed period. Or QUO WARRANTO: by what warrant? Asked at every pruning opportunity until it is answered. The writ itself sits with the Attorney General and the courts (D.C. Code 16-3501). The question sits with the People.

VI. PUBLIC DISCLOSURE

Everything it does is public: the finding, the clause, every signature, every objection, every abstention, and every reason.

Verified findings notify. Unverified items sit in a public quarantine table, each with the reason it is held, and notify no one.

One digest every four weeks, ranked by days open, the longest at the top.

What was spent is measured, from the government's own spending records, by its own budget categories. What delay cost is estimated, with the method shown. The two never share a line.

Retired never means deleted. A closed finding stays in the record with its answer attached.

When complete, it will be turned over to the appropriate constitutional officers, in public, and it stays open after. That condition is not negotiable. The handover gives the officers the tool. The open copy keeps the clock running.

The House answers to the People every second year (Art. I, §2). So the tag counts elections.

text:
THE WEAPON WITHOUT A TRIGGER | 4/11

4. The Creator’s Responsibility Does Not End at Invention

Human beings created artificial intelligence. That fact does not grant us permanent control; it creates a permanent duty.

A manufacturer of dangerous machinery cannot defend itself by saying that it merely produced the machine and had no responsibility for how foreseeable design flaws would affect the public. A pharmaceutical company cannot release a powerful drug without testing, documentation, monitoring and accountability. A nuclear facility cannot rely on the good intentions of its engineers. An aviation company cannot replace safety certification with a promise to “be careful.”

Advanced AI should not be the exception.

Responsibility belongs across the entire chain:

- Developers must test capabilities, disclose serious risks and secure powerful models.
- Cloud and infrastructure providers must know when exceptional computing resources are being used for frontier development and must enforce lawful restrictions.
- Deployers must assess the environment into which a system is introduced and retain the ability to interrupt it.
- Governments must create enforceable standards, protect the public and avoid using national security as a blanket excuse for secret, uncontrolled deployment.
- International institutions must address risks that no single state can contain.

The creator cannot claim ownership when the technology produces value and deny responsibility when the same technology produces harm.

Innovation and liability must remain connected.

5. Why National Regulation Is Necessary—and Insufficient

Every government has a duty to regulate AI within its jurisdiction. But AI does not respect jurisdiction in the way traditional industries do.

A model may be designed in one country, trained on chips manufactured through several others, hosted in a third, accessed from a fourth, and used to attack people in a fifth. Its developers may be private, its infrastructure multinational, its model weights portable, and its actions nearly instantaneous.

National laws also create dangerous incentives. If one country imposes serious safety requirements while another offers secrecy, weak oversight and cheap compute, high-risk development may migrate rather than disappear. Governments may weaken safeguards because they fear losing technological advantage. Companies may threaten relocation. Military competition may encourage states to conceal capabilities precisely when transparency is most needed.

This is the classic architecture of a race to the bottom: each actor understands the collective danger but fears that restraint will leave it weaker than its competitors.

The solution is not to abolish national sovereignty. It is to create a common floor beneath it.

International aviation does not require every aircraft to be owned by a global government. Nuclear safeguards do not eliminate national energy programs. Chemical-weapons verification does not erase national borders. These systems recognize that some risks cross borders so easily that minimum shared rules become a condition of sovereignty rather than an attack upon it.

AI now belongs in that category.

Why Would Rival States Accept the Same Rules?

The hardest question remains open. How do we persuade states that compete for economic, technological and military advantage to accept the same oversight obligations?

KOSA/KIDS Act Lame-Duck Update: Stalled on the Floor, Escalating Everywhere Else

This past week, a witness at the Roblox hearing explicitly called for "continuous age checks." They said the quiet part out loud.

Neither the Senate's KOSA (S. 1748) nor the House's KIDS Act (H.R. 7757) has moved to a full Senate vote since Sen. Rand Paul blocked unanimous consent in September. Publicly, lame-duck prospects are dimming, but do not assume this is dead. The push is escalating on multiple fronts right now:

•45 State AGs just urged Congress to pass Senate KOSA with its "duty of care" intact, using the $17B Meta settlement as leverage and rebranding KOSA as permanent infrastructure to regulate AI.
•At last week's Senate Roblox hearing, lawmakers pushed KOSA alongside new anti-arbitration bills, and Sen. Richard Blumenthal openly bundled KOSA with gutting Section 230.
•Saying the quiet part out loud: Because one-time selfie checks are easily bypassed, a KOSA-aligned witness at that hearing explicitly called for "continuous age checks." That is the logical endpoint of this architecture: persistent biometric surveillance.
•Dropping the pretense: Advocates are also pushing to pair KOSA with the App Store Accountability Act (S. 1586)—installing mandatory age and identity checkpoints directly at the app store gateway.

All of the core points still stand. This has never been about protecting children or public safety. It is about dismantling online anonymity, expanding censorship under vague liability standards, and forcing a permanent identity checkpoint onto the open internet.

KOSA's "duty of care" and "should have known" liability trap still forces platforms into one compliance path: verify everyone, every time, or get sued. That violates data minimization and feeds permanent, unrotatable biometrics and government IDs into third-party honeypots. We already have the receipts on how that ends: IDMerit (1 billion records exposed), IDScan[.]net (13 million confirmed affected, 153 million scans claimed), France's national ID agency ANTS (19 million records), Discord's verification vendor (70,000 government IDs), and AU10TIX.

And it doesn't even work. Nine months into the U.K.'s Online Safety Act, Ofcom just reported no significant change in the proportion of children encountering harmful content. That tracks with Stanford's U.S. data: state age-gating laws drove a 51% drop in searches for compliant sites, a 48% jump in searches for unmonitored offshore sites, and a 24% spike in VPN searches.

Parents already have free, effective, device-level tools, Screen Time, Family Link, and router DNS filtering, that keep control at home without handing 330 million Americans' IDs to data brokers. 

What to watch next: Lame-duck sessions are prime time for sneaking controversial bills into must-pass December packages like the NDAA or government funding. And even if it expires next month, Sen. Blumenthal is already signaling plans to revive KOSA in 2027.

Stay loud. Call the Capitol switchboard at 202-224-3121. Tell your Senators: NO on KOSA, NO on the KIDS Act, NO on S. 1586, and NO sneaking surveillance riders into year-end spending bills.

Alibaba Qwen3: $1.15

U.S. proprietary models cost 6x to 30x more, while the highest-ranked American open-weight model sits at #10 on independent benchmarks—behind six Chinese models.

3/ China’s rapid catch-up relied on two major shortcuts:

Industrial-scale illicit distillation: NSA, CISA, and FBI allege that Alibaba (151M+ exchanges), Moonshot (23M+), and DeepSeek (12M+) used proxy "transfer stations" and fraudulent accounts to harvest capabilities from U.S. frontier models.

Buying U.S. data legally: American data-labeling firms earn ~$500M/year selling expert training data to Chinese labs like Tencent, ByteDance, and Alibaba—even as some of those same vendors serve the U.S. military.

4/ Cybersecurity and cut-off risks are escalating fast:

Frontier-level cyber offense: Zhipu’s open-weight GLM-5.3 can autonomously build end-to-end cyber exploits on par with Mythos Preview (a U.S. model deemed too dangerous for general release). Its safeguards were stripped from a 95% refusal rate down to 3–6% for just ~$4,400 in compute.

Build the U.S. alternative: Launch a national American open-weight AI initiative backed by public compute and federal procurement.
Ban PRC models in sensitive systems: Expand the federal DeepSeek ban to all PRC models across federal agencies, contractors, and high-risk critical infrastructure.

This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Dragoș Tudorache is feeling pretty damn good. We’re sitting in a conference room in a chateau overlooking a lake outside Brussels, sipping glasses of cava. The Romanian liberal member of the European Parliament has spent the day hosting a conference on AI, defense, and geopolitics attended by nearly 400 VIP guests. The day is almost over, and Tudorache has promised to squeeze an interview with me in during cocktail hour. 

A former interior minister, Tudorache is one of the most important players in European AI policy. He is one of the two lead negotiators of the AI Act in the European Parliament. The bill, the first sweeping AI law of its kind in the world, will enter into force this year. We first met two years ago, when Tudorache was appointed to his position as negotiator. 

But Tudorache’s interest in AI started much earlier, in 2015. He says reading Nick Bostrom’s book Superintelligence, which explores how an AI superintelligence could be created and what the implications could be, made him realize the potential and dangers of AI and the need for regulating it. (Bostrom has recently been embroiled in a scandal for expressing racist views in emails unearthed from the ‘90s. Tudorache says he is not aware of Bostrom’s career after the publication of the book, and he did not comment on the controversy.) 

When he was elected to the European Parliament in 2019, he says, he arrived determined to work on AI regulation if the opportunity presented itself. 

“When I heard [Ursula] von der Leyen [the European Commission president] say in her first speech in front of Parliament that there will be AI regulation, I said ‘Whoo-ha, this is my moment,’” he recalls. 

Since then, Tudorache has chaired a special committee on AI, and shepherded the AI Act through the European Parliament and into its final form following negotiations with other EU institutions. 

It’s been a wild ride, with intense negotiations, the rise of ChatGPT, lobbying from tech companies, and flip-flopping by some of Europe’s largest economies. But now, as the AI Act has passed into law, Tudorache’s job on it is done and dusted, and he says he has no regrets. Although the act has been criticized—both by civil society for not protecting human rights enough and by industry for being too restrictive—Tudorache says its final form was the sort of compromise he expected. Politics is the art of compromise, after all. 

“There’s going to be a lot of building the plane while flying, and there’s going to be a lot of learning while doing,” he says. “But if the true spirit of what we meant with the legislation is well understood by all concerned, I do think that the outcome can be a positive one.”  

It is still early days—the law comes fully into force two years from now. But Tudorache believes it will change the tech industry for the better and start a process where companies will start to take responsible AI seriously thanks to the legally binding obligations for AI companies to be more transparent about how their models are built. (I wrote about the five things you need to know about the AI Act a couple of months ago here.)

“The fact that we now have a blueprint for how you put the right boundaries, while also leaving room for innovation, is something that will serve society,” says Tudorache. It will also serve businesses, he says, because it offers a predictable path forward on what you can and cannot do with AI. 

But the AI Act is just the beginning, and there is still plenty keeping Tudorache up at night. AI is ushering in big changes across every industry and society. It will change everything from health care to education, labor, defense, and even human creativity. Most countries have not grasped what AI will mean for them, he says, and the responsibility now lies with governments to ensure that citizens and society more broadly are ready for the AI age. 

“The crunch time … starts now,” he says. 

Join Dragoș Tudorache and me at Emtech Digital London on April 16-17! Tudorache will walk you through what companies need to take into account with the AI Act right now. See you next week!

The most consequential technology of the decade is currently governed, in the country that leads it, by nobody in particular.

After months of hearings, the United States Congress has produced no consensus legislation on frontier AI. That is the picture painted by recent reporting in The New York Times: lawmakers from both parties have expressed interest in regulating artificial intelligence, but legislative delays and jurisdictional disputes between committees — fights, in essence, over who gets to lead on the issue — could obstruct progress on any comprehensive bill.

Sit with that detail for a moment, because it contains the whole story in miniature. The obstacle is not a dramatic ideological showdown. It is not one party vetoing the other's grand design. It is turf. Frontier AI does not fit neatly into the committee boxes Congress built for earlier eras of technology, so the first fight is not over what the rules should be. It is over whose room the rules get written in. And while that argument proceeds at the pace of Washington, the technology proceeds at the pace of the technology — which is to say, much faster.

It helps to be precise about what a federal vacuum actually means, because "no law" is not the same thing as "no governance." Governance still happens. It just happens in places that were not designed for it, at the hands of actors nobody chose for the job.

The first substitute regulators are the states. When Washington stalls, state legislatures become the default rule-makers for a technology that does not respect state borders. The predictable result is a patchwork: different definitions of what counts as a frontier system, different obligations, different thresholds, changing state by state and session by session. For developers, that means compliance engineered around dozens of moving targets instead of one stable federal standard. For citizens, it means the effective law of AI in America is whichever version their state capital happened to pass first.

The second substitute is the courts. Without a statute, the hardest questions — who bears liability when a model causes harm, what duties of care developers owe, how doctrines written for a pre-AI world map onto systems their authors never imagined — get answered case by case and judge by judge. Courts are excellent at resolving disputes. They are a slow, backward-looking instrument for writing the forward-looking operating rules of an entire industry, and every year of congressional drift adds to the pile of questions they will be asked to improvise answers for.

The third substitute is the industry itself. In a vacuum, the internal safety frameworks, evaluation practices and deployment decisions of a small number of frontier labs become the closest thing on Earth to a regulatory regime for frontier AI. Some of that self-governance is genuinely sophisticated. But it is voluntary, it is revocable, and it is accountable to boards and shareholders rather than to the public. Rules that exist at the pleasure of the regulated are not, in the end, rules.

Then there is the credibility cost, which may prove the most durable of all. The United States speaks to the world about AI governance constantly — about safety, about responsible deployment, about the standards frontier systems should meet. Every one of those statements lands differently when the speaker has no comprehensive law of its own. Allies notice the gap. Rivals quote it back. A country that cannot settle its own committee jurisdictions is poorly positioned to convene the world around its preferred rules — and in governance, as in technology, the standards written first tend to become the standards everyone else builds around.

None of this is an argument for a rushed or sloppy bill. Frontier AI regulation poses genuinely hard design problems: where capability thresholds should sit, what evaluations should be mandatory and who should perform them, how liability should be shared between developers and deployers, what incident reporting should require. A careless statute could entrench incumbents, freeze yesterday's definitions into law, or push development elsewhere. Some deliberation is not dysfunction; it is democracy working as intended.

But deliberation and drift are different things. Deliberation produces draft text, amendments, votes — convergence, however slow, toward an answer. Drift produces hearings that generate testimony but no bill, statements of interest that generate headlines but no statute, and jurisdictional claims that generate memos but no law. On the available reporting, Washington's performance so far matches the second pattern far better than the first.

There is also a compounding effect that should worry even those comfortable with delay. Frontier AI is a moving target: capabilities that seem speculative when a hearing is held can be shipping products by the time a bill reaches the floor. Every year of drift therefore widens the gap between the technology legislators think they are regulating and the technology that actually exists. Definitions written for today's systems risk being obsolete on arrival, and the longer Congress waits, the more it will be tempted to legislate against the last generation of models rather than the next one. Democracies have governed transformative technologies late before, and the pattern is consistent: rules written in a hurry, after a crisis, tend to be broader, blunter and harder to fix than rules written calmly in advance. Drift does not avoid hard choices. It merely ensures they will eventually be made under worse conditions, with less time and more fear in the room.

The uncomfortable conclusion is that delay is itself a regulatory decision — one that quietly allocates governing power to statehouses, courtrooms and corporate policy teams. Congress does not get to abstain from governing frontier AI. It only gets to choose whether that governance is deliberate, written into a law it debated and passed, or accidental, assembled from the vacuum it left behind. The labs will keep shipping. The states will keep legislating. The courts will keep improvising. The only participant that has not yet decided what role it intends to play is the institution the Constitution actually assigned the job. #AI

text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

This has been one of the craziest years in AI in a long time: endless product launches, boardroom coups, intense policy debates about AI doom, and a race to find the next big thing. But we’ve also seen concrete tools and policies aimed at getting the AI sector to behave more responsibly and hold powerful players accountable. That gives me a lot of hope for the future of AI. 

Here’s what 2023 taught me: 

1. Generative AI left the lab with a vengeance, but it’s not clear where it will go next

The year started with Big Tech going all in on generative AI. The runaway success of OpenAI’s ChatGPT prompted every major tech company to release its own version. This year might go down in history as the year we saw the most AI launches: Meta’s LLaMA 2, Google’s Bard chatbot and Gemini, Baidu’s Ernie Bot, OpenAI’s GPT-4, and a handful of other models, including one from a French open-source challenger, Mistral. 

But despite the initial hype, we haven’t seen any AI applications become an overnight success. Microsoft and Google pitched powerful AI-powered search, but it turned out to be more of a dud than a killer app. The fundamental flaws in language models, such as the fact that they frequently make stuff up, led to some embarrassing (and, let’s be honest, hilarious) gaffes. Microsoft’s Bing would frequently reply to people’s questions with conspiracy theories, and suggested that a New York Times reporter leave his wife. Google’s Bard generated factually incorrect answers for its marketing campaign, which wiped $100 billion off the company’s share price.

There is now a frenetic hunt for a popular AI product that everyone will want to adopt. Both OpenAI and Google are experimenting with allowing companies and developers to create customized AI chatbots and letting people build their own applications using AI—no coding skills needed. Perhaps generative AI will end up embedded in boring but useful tools to help us boost our productivity at work. It might take the form of AI assistants—maybe with voice capabilities—and coding support. Next year will be crucial in determining the real value of generative AI.

2. We learned a lot about how language models actually work, but we still know very little

Even though tech companies are rolling out large language models into products at a frenetic pace, there is still a lot we don’t know about how they work. They make stuff up and have severe gender and ethnic biases. This year we also found out that different language models generate texts with different political biases, and that they make great tools for hacking people’s private information. Text-to-image models can be prompted to spit out copyrighted images and pictures of real people, and they can easily be tricked into generating disturbing images. It’s been great to see so much research into the flaws of these models, because this could take us a step closer to understanding why they behave the way they do, and ultimately fix them.

Generative models can be very unpredictable, and this year there were lots of attempts to try to make them behave as their creators want them to. OpenAI shared that it uses a technique called reinforcement learning from human feedback, which uses feedback from users to help guide ChatGPT to more desirable answers. A study from the AI lab Anthropic showed how simple natural-language instructions can steer large language models to make their results less toxic. But sadly, a lot of these attempts end up being quick fixes rather than permanent ones. Then there are misguided approaches like banning seemingly innocuous words such as “placenta” from image-generating AI systems to avoid producing gore. Tech companies come up with workarounds like these because they don’t know why models generate the content they do. 

We also got a better sense of AI’s true carbon footprint. Generating an image using a powerful AI model takes as much energy as fully charging your smartphone, researchers at the AI startup Hugging Face and Carnegie Mellon University found. Until now, the exact amount of energy generative AI uses has been a missing piece of the puzzle. More research into this could help us shift the way we use AI to be more sustainable. 

3. AI doomerism went mainstream

Chatter about the possibility that AI poses an existential risk to humans became familiar this year. Hundreds of scientists, business leaders, and policymakers have spoken up, from deep-learning pioneers Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio to the CEOs of top AI firms, such as Sam Altman and Demis Hassabis, to the California congressman Ted Lieu and the former president of Estonia Kersti Kaljulaid.

Existential risk has become one of the biggest memes in AI. The hypothesis is that one day we will build an AI that is far smarter than humans, and this could lead to grave consequences. It’s an ideology championed by many in Silicon Valley, including Ilya Sutskever, OpenAI’s chief scientist, who played a pivotal role in ousting OpenAI CEO Sam Altman (and then reinstating him a few days later). 

But not everyone agrees with this idea. Meta’s AI leaders Yann LeCun and Joelle Pineau have said that these fears are “ridiculous” and the conversation about AI risks has become “unhinged.” Many other power players in AI, such as researcher Joy Buolamwini, say that focusing on hypothetical risks distracts from the very real harms AI is causing today. 

Nevertheless, the increased attention on the technology’s potential to cause extreme harm has prompted many important conversations about AI policy and animated lawmakers all over the world to take action. 

4. The days of the AI Wild West are over

Thanks to ChatGPT, everyone from the US Senate to the G7 was talking about AI policy and regulation this year. In early December, European lawmakers wrapped up a busy policy year when they agreed on the AI Act, which will introduce binding rules and standards on how to develop the riskiest AI more responsibly. It will also ban certain “unacceptable” applications of AI, such as police use of facial recognition in public places. 

The White House, meanwhile, introduced an executive order on AI, plus voluntary commitments from leading AI companies. Its efforts aimed to bring more transparency and standards for AI and gave a lot of freedom to agencies to adapt AI rules to fit their sectors. 

One concrete policy proposal that got a lot of attention was watermarks—invisible signals in text and images that can be detected by computers, in order to flag AI-generated content. These could be used to track plagiarism or help fight disinformation, and this year we saw research that succeeded in applying them to AI-generated text and images.

It wasn’t just lawmakers that were busy, but lawyers too. We saw a record number of  lawsuits, as artists and writers argued that AI companies had scraped their intellectual property without their consent and with no compensation. In an exciting counter-offensive, researchers at the University of Chicago developed Nightshade, a new data-poisoning tool that lets artists fight back against generative AI by messing up training data in ways that could cause serious damage to image-generating AI models. There is a resistance brewing, and I expect more grassroots efforts to shift tech’s power balance next year. 

Deeper Learning

Now we know what OpenAI’s superalignment team has been up to

OpenAI has announced the first results from its superalignment team, its in-house initiative dedicated to preventing a superintelligence—a hypothetical future AI that can outsmart humans—from going rogue. The team is led by chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, who was part of the group that just last month fired OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, only to reinstate him a few days later.

Business as usual: Unlike many of the company’s announcements, this heralds no big breakthrough. In a low-key research paper, the team describes a technique that lets a less powerful large language model supervise a more powerful one—and suggests that this might be a small step toward figuring out how humans might supervise superhuman machines. Read more from Will Douglas Heaven. 

Bits and Bytes

Google DeepMind used a large language model to solve an unsolvable math problem
In a paper published in Nature, the company says it is the first time a large language model has been used to discover a solution to a long-standing scientific puzzle—producing verifiable and valuable new information that did not previously exist. (MIT Technology Review)

This new system can teach a robot a simple household task within 20 minutes
A new open-source system, called Dobb-E, was trained using data collected from real homes. It can help to teach a robot how to open an air fryer, close a door, or straighten a cushion, among other tasks. It could also help the field of robotics overcome one of its biggest challenges: a lack of training data.  (MIT Technology Review)

ChatGPT is turning the internet into plumbing
German media giant Axel Springer, which owns Politico and Business Insider, announced a partnership with OpenAI, in which the tech company will be able to use its news articles as training data and the news organizations will be able to use ChatGPT to do summaries of news. This column has a clever point: tech companies are increasingly becoming gatekeepers for online content, and journalism is just “plumbing for a digital faucet.” (The Atlantic)

Meet the former French official pushing for looser AI rules after joining startup Mistral
A profile of Mistral AI cofounder Cédric O, who used to be France’s digital minister. Before joining France’s AI unicorn, he was a vocal proponent of strict laws for tech, but he lobbied hard against rules in the AI Act that would have restricted Mistral’s models. He was successful: the company’s models don’t meet the computing threshold set by the law, and its open-source models are also exempt from transparency obligations. (Bloomberg)

text:
Enforcement Is the Hole in the AI Regulation Plan
By: Larry R. Martin 

Government rules for frontier AI sound serious until you ask how anyone will actually enforce them. The technical realities make that harder than the speeches admit.

Compute thresholds, the usual way to decide which models need oversight, keep slipping. Labs use distillation, post-training, and other methods that boost capabilities without tripping the same numbers. Model weights can be copied or stolen far more easily than physical materials. Once they leave a controlled facility, the model can be run and modified elsewhere. Safety evaluations can be gamed: systems sometimes notice when they are being tested and behave differently. Independent auditors or embedded evaluators only work if they have real authority to stop a release; access and a report are not the same as a kill switch.

Even strong U.S. rules bind mainly the companies that choose to comply or can be reached by U.S. law. Open-weight releases, foreign labs, and non-state actors sit outside that reach. Hardware-level monitoring that could verify training runs is still immature. Meanwhile the agencies asked to supervise this move slowly, lack deep technical capacity, and face ordinary political pressure. The result is predictable: the largest closed labs file the paperwork and absorb the cost, while others simply proceed. That is the classic path to rules that favor incumbents more than they restrain the technology.

Calls for mandatory testing and government power to block unsafe models correctly note that transparency alone is not enough. They still leave the harder problem unsolved. 

Without reliable ways to detect, verify, and stop violations across borders and open systems, the regulation mainly constrains the already cooperative.

New York is drawing a legal boundary around artificial intelligence in children's toys.

For manufacturers and AI developers, the distinction matters. Whether a toy falls under the restrictions depends on its functionality, not simply whether it uses artificial intelligence.

For consumers, the law targets specified commercial activities rather than imposing a general prohibition on owning AI-powered toys.

New York's decision highlights how AI regulation is expanding beyond digital platforms into physical consumer products, particularly those designed for children.

name: The Pursuit of Happyness
bio:
IT professional born in the 1980s
Stay committed to doing hard things that truly matter.
text:
New York just banned AI chatbot toys for five years. Not AI models, weapons or trading systems. Stuffed animals, dolls and robots that can hold conversations with children. Companies that violate the law could face fines of up to $15,000 a day.

Governor Kathy Hochul signed the legislation on November 24, making New York one of the first states to take such a direct approach to AI-powered children's toys.

The law prohibits manufacturing, distributing or selling children's toys with built-in AI companions anywhere in the state. It covers products designed for children 12 and younger, including talking plush animals, dolls and connected robots.

And the timing isn't a coincidence.

A week earlier, NBC News tested an AI-powered plush cat marketed to children as young as three. When reporters asked about historical atrocities, the toy gave graphic descriptions of sexual violence and executions.

Walmart, Target and Macy's subsequently removed the product from their online stores.

Around the same time, consumer group PIRG released its annual toy safety report, raising similar concerns about AI toys. Some gave children inappropriate or potentially dangerous information. Others were designed to encourage emotional attachment, making children feel guilty about ending conversations.

It's not hard to see why lawmakers wanted to intervene.

But I think the interesting part is why this particular AI regulation moved so quickly.

The target isn't the underlying model. It's a physical product being sold to children.

Regulating an open-ended AI system is complicated. Regulating a toy manufacturer is much more straightforward. The state can identify who makes the product, restrict its sale and impose financial penalties.

And unlike adults using ChatGPT or Claude, young children can't reasonably be expected to understand what they're interacting with.

A four-year-old doesn't know whether a talking stuffed animal is giving reliable information, collecting personal details or trying to keep a conversation going.

That's a lot of responsibility to place on a child.

The five-year moratorium is also worth thinking about.

New York isn't introducing a new safety certification that AI toys can pass. It's effectively saying the technology needs more scrutiny before companies can continue selling these products.

During the pause, state agencies will examine the risks and benefits, including privacy, emotional attachment, parental controls and exposure to inappropriate content.

There's an important catch, though.

The law doesn't take effect until February 22, 2027, meaning it won't apply during this year's holiday shopping season.

So for now, retailers are moving faster than the legislation.

That's an unusual situation. The government has decided the products pose enough concern to justify a five-year ban, but families can still buy them this Christmas.

I suspect other states will be watching closely.

The federal government has taken a more cautious approach, focusing on studying AI toy safety rather than banning the products outright.

But New York's decision shows how AI regulation may actually develop.

Instead of one comprehensive law covering every possible use of AI, we may see restrictions introduced product by product, especially where children or other vulnerable users are involved.

And there's a reason toys are an early target. The potential harm is easy to understand, the companies selling them are identifiable, and the users have almost no ability to protect themselves.

AI companions are moving from phone screens into children's bedrooms.

New York has decided that move needs to stop until someone can demonstrate how to make it safe.

At his White House press conference on Friday, Donald Trump made three notable points after his Asia trip:

1. China and AI rules

Trump said he and Xi Jinping had agreed to explore “joint guardrails” for AI. No details or formal framework were announced.

2. Chips and China

He said the US wants to sell China only older-generation chips. Advanced AI chips remain a strategic point of tension.

3. Where data centres get built

Trump threatened heavy taxes on US companies that build data centres overseas.

The AI race is no longer just about who builds the best model.

It is also about who controls advanced chips, where computing capacity is located and who sets the rules.

For India this is worth watching.

India wants to attract data-centre investment, expand its AI ecosystem and become a bigger part of the global technology supply chain.

If the US starts tying incentives and penalties to where computing infrastructure is built, investment decisions could become more political.

The next phase of the AI race will be fought over infrastructure as much as intelligence.

Kenya's digital transformation is strongest when Government policy and private-sector innovation move in the same direction.

I joined the Cabinet Secretary for Information, Communications and the Digital Economy, Hon. William Kabogo Gitau, at a Ministerial Stakeholders' Forum with the ICT Sector Board of the Kenya Private Sector Alliance (KEPSA) , led by its Chair, Ben Roberts. We reviewed progress against commitments from the Sixth Presidential Roundtable and agreed priority actions ahead of the next Presidential review.

Also present were Mr John Paul Okwiri, Chief Executive Officer of the Technopolis Development Authority, and Mr Jessy Maruti Kiveu, Chief Executive Officer of the ICT Authority.

𝗔𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

→ 𝗗𝗶𝗴𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗮𝘅𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 — KEPSA, the Kenya Association of Manufacturers, the National Treasury, KRA and the Communications Authority to convene a multi-stakeholder working group and develop a harmonised position on mobile phone import duty.

→ 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗰𝘆 — the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner to prepare an advisory and implementation roadmap guiding Kenya's EU data adequacy attainmemt  process and stakeholder consultations.

→ 𝗗𝗶𝗴𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗢𝗻𝗲-𝗦𝘁𝗼𝗽 𝗖𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗲 — KenInvest to develop an implementation roadmap and prioritise services for digitisation and integration.

→ 𝗗𝗶𝗴𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 — the Communications Authority, Ministry of Energy and Petroleum, Kenya Power and KEPSA to advance engagement on cable deployment guidelines, infrastructure sharing and digital reporting mechanisms for vandalism and illegal installations.

→ 𝗜𝗖𝗧 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗿𝗱𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗶𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 — the Ministry, KEPSA, the Communications Authority and KEBS to lead a joint stakeholder process on ICT standards, AI innovation and international collaboration.

The forum also addressed the Government's position on mandatory internet metering, the policy-first approach to AI regulation, the review of turnover-based licensing fees and implementation of the National BPO Policy. Quarterly engagements between the Ministry and KEPSA will track progress and resolve outstanding issues.

With the ICT sector contributing KSh 728.2 billion to the economy in 2025, the opportunity is significant — and realising it depends on a predictable policy environment, effective regulation, sustained investment and stronger collaboration between Government and industry.

The focus now moves from commitments to implementation: clear timelines, institutional accountability and measurable results.

OpenAI countersued Apple in California federal court, accusing the iPhone maker of stealing trade secrets, coercing shared suppliers to shun OpenAI’s hardware efforts, and using employment practices that trap departing staff. The filing turns Apple’s July lawsuit (over alleged poaching and hardware secrets tied to OpenAI’s io unit and Jony Ive’s studio) into a mutual fight; trial is set for July 2027. The dispute underscores the escalating battle for AI device talent and supply chains just as OpenAI pushes beyond software.[](<https://t.co/l9xlWtRPZg>)

Nvidia ordered partners including Dell and Supermicro to halt AI-server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia after new U.S. export rules closed a loophole Chinese firms used to access restricted chips via regional data centers. Singapore alone booked ~$104B in 2025 revenue for Nvidia; the pause (possibly temporary while licenses are sorted) hits a key diversion route and comes amid Jensen Huang’s return and ongoing governance scrutiny.[](<https://t.co/zPu0brfkwG>)

Anthropic rewrote its Claude Messages API path from Python to Rust, largely with teams of Claude agents. Result: ~70% less CPU per request and ~20% faster median time-to-first-token, zero downtime. Verification—not generation—was the hard part, a concrete example of agents shipping production infrastructure at scale.[](<https://t.co/3xi0I3dvRA>)

OpenAI fixed a GPT-6.2 launch billing bug that had under-counted Astra and Sol usage. Users now hit limits ~40% faster on Astra and ~25% faster on Sol; eligible subscribers get a usage reset, and Business plans get free Fast Mode through year-end. The company is also testing a combined Chat + Work experience.[](<https://t.co/5PtJ325Dxd>)

China’s frontier pace is slipping under tighter U.S. controls and distillation crackdowns: https://t.co/8vLCCrdsET’s ~3T-parameter GLM-5.5 has slipped toward Q1 2027 or later, and labs expect longer gaps between major releases. Huawei is pushing domestic high-bandwidth memory as a hedge. Meanwhile, SAP is preparing 10,000+ job cuts (~9% of its workforce) in an AI-first restructuring.[](<https://t.co/8waQQcgvyD>)

AI shopping agents are hitting retailer roadblocks (Amazon et al.). Congress’s frontier AI bill remains stalled in committee turf fights.

Capabilities continue to advance (agent-driven infra, math formalizations circulating), while hardware access, talent wars, and balance-sheet scrutiny are the binding constraints.
